analysis.one_liner: Cuts individual income tax rates, repeals the top 39.6% rate, and ends limits on high earners' deductions and exemptions.
analysis.headline: The Republican tax cut bill was introduced in late November 1994, sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut federal income tax rates for individuals. It eliminated the top 39.6% rate and scheduled step-downs in every bracket between 1995 and 1998, ending at a 12%/22%/25%/33% structure. It also repealed two rules that raise taxes on higher earners: the cap on how much of their itemized deductions wealthy taxpayers lose, and the phaseout of personal exemptions at high incomes. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains would go to taxpayers with the highest incomes. The 39.6% rate applied only to income above $250,000 for couples ($125,000 single), so repealing it exclusively benefits people in that range. The lower brackets would help all taxpayers somewhat, but the repeal of the itemized-deduction cap and the personal-exemption phaseout — both of which apply only at high incomes — adds benefits concentrated at the top.

how_it_helps.text: It strikes the 39.6% top rate from the tax tables, so income at the very top would be taxed at 33% or less.
It schedules rate cuts over four years: by 1998 the brackets drop to 12%, 22%, 25%, and 33%.
It repeals the overall limitation on itemized deductions and the phaseout of personal exemptions, rules that apply mainly to high-income taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: All taxpayers indirectly, through a larger federal deficit: rate cuts of this size without offsetting spending cuts must be borrowed, and future taxpayers bear the interest. The overall mix of benefits tilts away from low- and middle-income households.

drawbacks.text: The bill cut the top rate from 39.6% to 33% and phased rates down over four years, a reduction that concentrates its dollar benefit on the highest earners and increases the federal deficit, since it includes no offsetting revenue.

Repealing the limits on itemized deductions and the personal-exemption phaseout further tilts the benefit toward taxpayers with large incomes, since deduction caps and exemption phaseouts apply mainly at higher income levels.
The bill explicitly shields the rate cuts from being treated as a rate change for budget-enforcement purposes, limiting the normal mechanisms that would flag its fiscal cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For high-income households, the benefit was large and immediate. But the bill contained no spending cuts or revenue offsets, so its cost was higher deficits — a bill ultimately paid for by future taxpayers and through pressure on government programs — with only a small slice of the rate cuts reaching middle- and lower-income families. An honest supporter would acknowledge the regressivity; an honest opponent would note the top rate had been raised just the year before.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee in the final days of the Congress, and the committee never acted, so it expired without a vote when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 29, 1994 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.
No further action was recorded: the committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it never reached the House floor.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, killing all legislation not enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death except, in a fiscal sense, the federal treasury and future taxpayers, who were spared the cost of unfinanced rate cuts. High earners lost a potential tax cut; the existing top rate and deduction limits stayed in place.

for.name: Rep. Newt Gingrich, Rep. Dick Armey, and Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats supported the bill, and a Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never took it up.

industries.industry: High-income individuals and households (top earners above ~$250,000)
industries.note: The bill removes the 39.6% top bracket and lowers every upper rate, concentrating its largest dollar savings on the wealthiest taxpayers. Repealing deduction limits and the exemption phaseout adds to the benefit at the top.
A wholesale re-writing of the rate tables and brackets would create new planning demand, though this is a secondary effect of any major tax change.
